newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Force commander rules out disarming Hutu militia.
newsitem.headline: Force commander rules out disarming Hutu militia.

text.p: The Canadian force commander for troops planning to deliver humanitarian aid to eastern Zaire on Thursday ruled out disarming militia lodged in refugee camps or separating them from civilians.

At a news conference, Lt.-Gen. Maurice Baril as well as Canadia's deputy foreign minister Gordon Smith said the troops, estimated to eventually reach over 10,000 soldiers, would not use force unless they were attacked.
U.N. officials said earlier feeding areas would be set up by the troops and that no armed militia would be allowed to enter. But Baril made no mention of this.

"The immediate issue is that of providing relief to the people who are displaced. And that means providing the security so that the humanitarian organisations can deliver aid," Smith said. "The second thing, and it is very important, is to create the necessary conditions for the voluntary, orderly and secure repatriation of refugees."

"But let me say directly one of the elements that this mission would not comprise, and that is separating militias or intimidators in camps from other civilians who might wish to return to Rwanda or Burundi (or) to disarm the so-called intimidators," he said.

"In order to do so, the level of violence that would occur would be really very high and the people that would be killed would not only be the soldiers of the contributing countries but would be in many cases innocent refugees -- women and children."
Baril said a Canadian reconnaissance mission left on Thursday for eastern Zaire and Americans had been in neighbouring Rwanda earlier to send back intelligence on the troops.

About 1.5 million refugees, mainly Hutus, fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates. The eastern Zairean province of Kivu has remained politically tense since then, with a new war breaking out in September between Tutsi residents of Zaire and local Zaireans backed by Zaire's army.
U.S. troops will be in Goma in the northern part of Kivu province, while sources said French and British troops may be at Bukavu airport in the southern part of the province.

Baril was in New York to speak to potential troop contributors and Canadian officials said they had received widespread responses. The U.N. Security Council is expected to put its seal of approval on the force, not organised under a U.N. command, on Friday.
Diplomats said the initial forces expected in the region would come from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal.

A fund is expected to set up for other African nations such as Cameroon, Ethiopia, Eritrea and others but Baril stressed all would have to be self-contained units with logistics. Envoys said Egypt, Belgium, Ireland, Brazil and Portugal have volunteered troops and Norway and Finland may send human rights observers.
To encourage Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire to return home to Rwanda, the United Nations has suggested human rights monitors in Rwanda be increased from 110 to about 300, the diplomats added.

Baril said he would establish main headquarters in Goma which is partly, if not entirely, destroyed. Therefore he would have "rear elements" of his headquarters in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda, and Kinshasa, the capital of Zaire.

He said he intended to establish staging bases for the force, which eventually would number more than 10,000 troops, in Kigali, Entebbe in Uganda and Nairobi, the Kenyan capital with two "secure forward operations bases" in Goma and Bukavu in eastern Zaire.

Baril said "self-contained units would radiate outward from those forward operating bases to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid." Land corridors would be opened from Rwanda, Uganda or Kenya for the supplies and the soldiers.

The United States, which will field up to 1,000 soldiers in eastern Zaire and up to 4,000 more in various neighbouring countries, also wants humanitarian corridors to encourage Hutu refugees to return to Rwanda. But Baril said the force would not be responsible for "overall repatriation."
